doc.title: Bob Cranshaw interviewed by Michael Woods, New York City, New York, October 18, 1995

title: Playing by ear and learning to read; Monty Alexander and Erroll Garner
summary: Learning to read took hard work, but his ear lets him follow players like Monty Alexander and Erroll Garner through key changes; he can work from notes, changes or ear.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: frightened as to what, you know, music in front of you, then that’s another story because it’s there so you don’t have a chance to do you know those things. And it took me a long time to really learn to read because I had depended upon my ear for so many years that it took again, a lot of practice to learn to read. But I was determined that I was going to win that battle also. And I did. But the ear part has just helped me, especially with the jazz things. I just, again, I don’t, I play what I hear. I know the chords and things to the tune, but I can follow. You can go where you want to go, you can change keys, you can do whatever you like to do. I would rather you not tell me ‘cause I’m not thinking about it. I’m only thinking about what I hear, you know. So working with a lot of piano players like Monty Alexander and working with Erroll Garner and people like that who play by ear. I mean Monty and I, we would play and start a tune in one key, and we could end up in another key, and not really, we didn’t really think about it. It was nothing that we thought we were in another key, it felt like the key that we were in. I mean we would just go off on tangents with just playing. And it was wonderful for me because it gave me a chance to use — God I feel gave me the talent and the ear to be able to hear, so I didn’t see any reason why not to use it. It is that I have to use it with the academics. Then I finally got into that and I got really deep into it, so I’m thankful that I did, now, with the studio things and being able to do other things besides just play what I hear or being intimidated by going someplace and they put music there and, oh my God, I can’t read it, you know.
So in other words, you can go all three ways. If they give you notes, if they give you changes, or if they just ask you to hear the forms.
